An open-ended question is one that does not provide predefined response options for the participant to choose from. 4. Ordinal categorical data refers to categorical data where the variables can be ranked or ordered hierarchically. For example, the number of children a woman has is an ordinal categorical variable. 5. The p-value represents the probability that an observed difference or association could have occurred purely by chance. 6. Parametric tests are statistical tests that are applicable when the data follows a normal distribution, meaning it is symmetrically distributed around the mean, forming a bell-shaped or Gaussian curve. 7. A peer-reviewed journal is a publication in which articles are evaluated by independent experts for quality and relevance, making it highly credible. 8. Phase I clinical trials are the initial studies of a new drug or formulation in humans, often conducted in healthy volunteers, to evaluate therapeutic activity and short-term safety. 9. Phase III clinical trials involve larger and more diverse patient groups to assess the balance of shortand long-term safety and efficacy, as well as the overall therapeutic value of the drug. 10. Phase IV clinical trials are conducted after a pharmaceutical product is marketed to identify rare or long-term side effects. 11. A pie chart is a graphical representation of categorical data frequencies in the form of a circular pie divided into segments. 12. A pilot study is a preliminary investigation to test the feasibility of a study protocol before the main study is conducted. It is also referred to as a pre-test. 13. The placebo effect occurs when participants in a study experience perceived or actual improvement in their condition after receiving an inert substance, likely due to their expectations. 14. A population is the entire group of individuals, animals, objects, or events that a researcher intends to study. 15. A positive correlation between two variables means that as one variable increases, the other also increases. 16. Statistical power refers to the probability of correctly rejecting the null hypothesis when the alternative hypothesis is true, indicating the likelihood of detecting an effect if it exists. 17. Predictive value is the frequency with which a positive diagnostic test result accurately indicates the presence of a disease. 18. A pre-test is a preliminary study conducted to evaluate the feasibility and appropriateness of a questionnaire before the main study. 19. A pre-test/post-test design is an experimental research method where measurements are taken both before and after an intervention. 20. Prevalence refers to the total occurrence of a specific condition within a defined population at a particular point in time. 21. Probability is the likelihood of an event occurring, ranging from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). Researchers must define the level of probability they are willing to accept for their findings. 22. Proportion is the ratio of one value to another, expressed as a fraction. For example, the proportion of women among patients with cardiovascular disease. 23. A proposal is a document written to secure funding for a research project. 24. A protocol is the detailed written plan of a study, which is essential for any research project. 25. PubMed Central is a publicly accessible online archive providing free access to peer-reviewed primary research reports in the life sciences, funded by the US National Institutes of Health. 26. Quality assurance is a system ensuring that a study is conducted and data is generated, recorded, and reported in compliance with the protocol, good clinical practice, and national regulations. 27. Qualitative methods focus on non-numerical data and interpretive analysis. 28. Quantitative methods emphasize the collection of numerical data or data that can be quantified, followed by statistical analysis. 29. A questionnaire is a tool for collecting data from individuals, either through open-ended questions (allowing free responses) or closed questions (with predefined answer options). 30. Random sampling is a method of selecting a sample from a population where each member has an equal chance of being chosen. It is not the same as haphazard sampling. 31. Randomized controlled trials are intervention studies where participants are prospectively assigned to experimental or control groups using a random method. 32. The range in a dataset is the difference between the highest and lowest scores. 33. A ratio is a numerical expression of the relationship between two sets of frequencies, such as the ratio of males to females in a sample. 34. A rate is a numerical expression of the frequency of a condition within a given population over a specified time period. 35. A regression equation describes the relationship between two variables, indicating how changes in one variable correspond to average changes in the other. 36. A regression line is a line on a scatter plot that illustrates the degree and direction of the correlation between two variables. 37. The regression coefficient quantifies the amount by which a change in one variable must be multiplied to yield the corresponding average change in the other variable. 38. Regression to the mean is a phenomenon where extreme scores tend to move closer to the average upon re-measurement. 39. Relative risk is the ratio of the incidence of an outcome in an exposed group to the incidence in an unexposed group. 40. Reliability refers to the consistency or reproducibility of a test or measurement result. 41. A representative sample accurately reflects the characteristics of the population from which it is drawn. 42. A retrospective study is an observational study design that examines past and present events. 43. Risk factors are variables believed to increase the likelihood of a specific outcome or illness. 44. The Rosenthal effect occurs when researchers' expectations influence the outcome of a study. 45. A sample is a subset of the population selected for study. 46. Sampling error is the discrepancy between values obtained from a sample and the larger population from which the sample was drawn. 47. A scatter diagram is a graph that displays the relationship between two variables, providing an indication of whether a correlation exists and its direction. 48. Selection bias is a systematic difference between individuals selected for a study and those not selected. 49. A skewed distribution is an asymmetrical frequency distribution curve with one side elongated. 50. Specificity is the proportion of individuals who test negative for a disease among those who do not have the disease. 51. Standard deviation measures the dispersion or variability of a group of scores. 52. Standard error is a statistical measure of the likelihood that a sample finding reflects the population finding. 53. Statistical significance indicates that an observed result is unlikely to be due to chance and is likely real. However, it does not necessarily imply importance or interest. 54. A statistical significance test estimates the probability that an observed study result, such as a difference between groups or an association, is due to chance. 55. Stratified random sampling ensures that important subgroups within a population are adequately represented in the sample. 56. A structured interview involves predefined questions asked in a fixed order and recorded systematically. 57. Subjective measures involve a significant degree of human interpretation, such as pain ratings. 58. Subjects are participants in a study and should not be referred to as material for the study. 59. A surrogate endpoint is a variable that is relatively easy to measure and predicts a rare or distant outcome but is not a direct measure of harm or clinical benefit. 60. Systematic sampling involves selecting subjects using a simple periodic process, such as choosing every second or third patient. 61. The 10/90 gap highlights that while 90% of the global disease burden is in developing countries, only about 10% of global resources are allocated to addressing these issues. 62. A transcript is a verbatim written record of an interview. 63. A true negative occurs when a diagnostic test correctly identifies that a person does not have a disease. 64. A true positive occurs when a diagnostic test correctly identifies that a person has a disease. 65. A two-tailed test is a statistical test that examines differences between two groups without assuming the direction of the difference. It requires a larger sample size than a one-tailed test. 66. A Type I error occurs when a statistical test incorrectly concludes that there is an association or difference in the population when none exists. The probability of this error is represented by alpha (α), also known as the level of statistical significance. 67. A Type II error occurs when a statistical test fails to detect an association or difference in the population when one actually exists. The probability of this error is represented by beta (β). 68. Unlinked information refers to data that cannot be associated with the individual it pertains to, ensuring confidentiality is not compromised. 69. Univariate analysis involves mathematical tools to assess the relationship between one independent variable and one dependent variable. 70. Validity is the extent to which a test measures what it is intended to measure. 71. Variability describes the extent to which a group of scores varies or is spread out, often represented by descriptive statistics such as range or standard deviation. 72. A variable is a statistical term for a data point or score. 73. Variance measures the dispersion or variability of a group of scores.
